presentingComplaint: Progressive fatigue, breathlessness on exertion, and unsteady gait for the past 3 months, with tingling and numbness in both feet for 6 weeks.
history: A 62-year-old man, strict vegetarian for over 30 years, presents with a 3-month history of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and low mood. Over the last 6 weeks he has developed symmetric numbness and tingling in both feet ascending toward the ankles, and his gait has become increasingly unsteady, worse in the dark or with eyes closed. His wife has noticed him becoming more forgetful and irritable. He denies overt GI bleeding, melena, or hematemesis, but reports intermittent glossitis and a sore tongue. No alcohol excess. No history of gastric or ileal surgery, but he mentions a family history of thyroid disease and was recently found to have mild vitiligo. No fever, no weight loss out of proportion to reduced appetite. No history of anticonvulsant, metformin, or proton-pump-inhibitor use beyond metformin for type 2 diabetes started 8 years ago.
examination: Pallor with mild scleral icterus (lemon-yellow tinge). Glossitis with a smooth, beefy-red tongue. Neurological exam: reduced vibration and proprioception in both lower limbs, absent ankle jerks with exaggerated knee jerks, bilateral extensor plantar responses (upgoing Babinski), positive Romberg sign, and a broad-based, unsteady (ataxic) gait. No papilledema. Mild cognitive slowing on bedside testing (MMSE 26/30). No hepatosplenomegaly. No lymphadenopathy. No signs of active bleeding.
imaging: MRI spine: T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord, consistent with subacute combined degeneration
differentialDiagnoses: Vitamin B12 deficiency with subacute combined degeneration of the cord
Guillain-Barre syndrome (for the ascending sensory/gait picture)
finalDiagnosis: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency due to pernicious anemia, presenting with macrocytic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
citations: Harrison 22e - Disorders of the Autonomic Nervous System and peripheral/dorsal column disease (subacute combined degeneration)
British Society for Haematology Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Cobalamin and Folate Disorders 2014
contraindications: Do not give folic acid alone before confirming/treating B12 deficiency - may correct hematologic picture while worsening or precipitating neurologic damage
Avoid delaying parenteral B12 replacement pending exhaustive workup once biochemical deficiency with neurologic signs is confirmed
edgeCases: Serum B12 can be falsely normal in early or mild deficiency; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are more sensitive functional markers
Neurologic manifestations (subacute combined degeneration) can occur without anemia or macrocytosis being present
Metformin use is an independent risk factor for B12 deficiency and may confound the vegetarian-diet attribution
Concurrent autoimmune conditions (vitiligo, thyroid disease) support an autoimmune pernicious anemia diathesis and warrant screening for other autoimmune endocrinopathies
